answers.topic: Emotions, expected emotions, and risk aversion
answers: They found that people badly overestimate how bad a loss will feel. Before the coin flip, participants expected losing three dollars to drop their happiness by about 4 points and winning five dollars to raise it by about 2 points. After the flip, the real drop was only about 1 point and the real rise about 1.2. So the loss hurt far less than predicted, because people forget about the coping mechanisms that switch on after a loss.

The outcome of a coin flip was what varied. Participants were given five dollars and told the flip would decide whether they won an extra five dollars or lost three. They rated their happiness first to set a baseline, then predicted how they would feel after winning or losing, and later reported how they actually felt, so the researchers could compare expected emotions with actual emotions.

Expected emotions are one of the things that determine risk aversion. Risk aversion is the tendency to avoid taking risks, and when you predict that a loss will make you feel terrible, you become less willing to take a chance that could lead to it. Because people believe a loss will hit harder than an equal gain would help, they avoid risks more than they should.

People overestimate it because they forget about their coping mechanisms. After a loss, we usually have ways of coping that get activated and soften how we really feel, but when we predict our emotions ahead of time, we do not take those into account. So the prediction misses by a lot, as in Kermer and colleagues (2006), where the real drop was far smaller than expected.

Flattened emotions make decisions worse. People with damage to part of the prefrontal cortex feel much less than usual, and their decision making is impaired, so emotion is part of deciding well. Anxiety leads people to avoid choices that could lead to large negative consequences, which is risk avoidance. Optimism leads people to ignore negative information and focus on the positive, and too much of it leads to poor decisions.

They found that cloudy weather changed how applicants were judged. Simonsohn (2007) looked at university admissions decisions and found that applicants' academic attributes were weighted more heavily on cloudy days than on sunny days. The weather had nothing to do with the applicants, yet it shifted what the decision makers paid most attention to. That makes weather an incidental factor from the surroundings.

He found that prospective students visiting a highly rated university were more likely to enroll if they had visited the campus on a cloudy day. Simonsohn (2009) is about enrollment, not admissions. The weather on a single visit says nothing about how good the school is, yet it carried into one of the biggest decisions a student makes.

What was manipulated was the mood participants were in before deciding, using a film clip. Lerner and colleagues (2004) had people watch one of three clips: a sad one showing a person dying, a disgust one showing a person using a dirty toilet, or a neutral one showing fish at the Great Barrier Reef. Then everyone set prices for a set of highlighters.

Both groups differed from the neutral group, but in different ways. For selling, the neutral group asked about 4.50 dollars, the disgust group about 2.70 and the sad group about 3.00. For buying, neutral offered about 3.50, disgust about 3.00 and sad about 4.50. So disgust lowered both prices, while sadness lowered the selling price but raised the buying price.

This is an example of an incidental emotion. The mood comes from a film clip, which has nothing to do with the highlighters, yet it changes what the highlighters seem worth. Incidental emotions are not specifically related to the decision itself. They can come from a person's disposition, a recent experience, or the surroundings, and they still influence what people decide.

answers.topic: Context, defaults, and the status quo bias
answers: The context that came before the same test case was manipulated. Physicians read a hypothetical case of a possible cesarean candidate, and the case itself never changed. In the control condition it came first, in another it came after four cases with serious complications, and in the third it came after four fairly routine, not serious cases. The question was whether the earlier cases changed the recommendation.

The physicians who had read the non-serious cases first recommended cesarean significantly more often. The test case was identical for everyone, so the cases they had just considered must have changed their judgment. After four routine cases, the test case looked serious by comparison, so more doctors recommended surgery. Even experts get swayed by the context their decision is made in.

In an opt-in procedure you have to take an active step to become an organ donor, and countries using it have less than a 28 percent consent rate. In an opt-out procedure you are a donor unless you request not to be, and those countries have over a 99 percent consent rate. The difference comes from what happens when people simply do nothing.

That is the status quo bias, which is the tendency to do nothing when faced with a difficult decision. If people leave the default organ donor choice unchanged, the default wins. Under opt-in, doing nothing means you are not a donor, and under opt-out, doing nothing means you are one. Many people do nothing either way, which is why the consent rates are so far apart.

In the gain frame, people mostly took the sure option. The disease was expected to kill 600 people, and the outcomes were described as people saved. Program A saved 200 for certain, and Program B gave a one in three chance of saving all 600 and a two in three chance of saving none. Seventy-two percent chose Program A, and 28 percent chose Program B.

In the loss frame, people mostly took the gamble. The same disease problem was worded in terms of people who die. Program C had 400 people dying for certain, and Program D gave a one in three chance that no one dies and a two in three chance that all 600 die. Seventy-eight percent chose Program D, and only 22 percent chose Program C.

They are the same outcome described in different words. Saving 200 of 600 people means that 400 die, so Program A and Program C come to exactly the same thing. Program B and Program D are also the same gamble. Only the wording changed, from people saved to people who die, and yet most people switched from the sure option to the gamble.

A gain frame encourages a risk-aversion strategy, meaning people prefer the sure option. A loss frame encourages a risk-taking strategy, meaning people prefer the gamble. This is the framing effect: the way a decision is stated highlights what might be gained or what might be lost, and the same people can switch strategies depending only on the wording.

Risk aversion is the tendency to avoid taking risks, which in the disease problem means choosing the sure option. Risk taking is going for the gamble, accepting uncertainty in the hope of a better result. Tversky and Kahneman (1981) showed that the same people can show either one, depending on whether the outcomes are framed as gains or as losses.

People rejected unfair offers much more often when they came from a human than from a computer. Sanfey and colleagues (2003) found that fair offers, five and five or seven and three, were accepted almost always from either partner. But an eight and two offer was accepted about 53 percent of the time from a human and about 85 percent from a computer, and nine and one about 37 percent versus 68 percent. People were less angry with an unfair computer.

Utility theory says the responder should accept any offer. It judges a choice by the value of its outcome, and even one dollar is worth more than the nothing you get by rejecting. If the responder rejects, neither player gets paid, so a responder following utility theory would never turn down money. The finding was that real people do not behave that way.

They found that people with more activation of the right anterior insula were more likely to reject more offers. The insula is an area connected with emotional states. People often rejected low offers because they became angry that the offers were unfair, and that anger cost them money. So the brain activity fits the idea that emotion is important in decision making.

Neuroeconomics combines research from psychology, neuroscience and economics. Psychology contributes how people think and feel, neuroscience contributes what happens in the brain, and economics contributes how choices about value are analyzed. Putting them together lets researchers study a decision and the brain activity behind it at the same time, including how emotions tied to specific brain areas influence choices.

answers.topic: Deductive reasoning, validity, and belief bias
answers: A syllogism is the basic form of deductive reasoning, introduced by Aristotle. It has two statements called premises, which are the statements the reasoning starts from, and a third statement called the conclusion, which is what you arrive at. The only question you ask is whether the conclusion follows from the two premises. For example, all birds are animals and all animals eat food, so all birds eat food.

Validity is about whether the conclusion follows logically from the premises, and it depends on the form of the reasoning. Truth is about whether the statements match the world. They can come apart. If the premises of a valid syllogism are true, the conclusion must be true, but a valid form with a false premise can still give a false conclusion.

Belief bias is the tendency to think a syllogism is valid just because its conclusion is believable. It means you judge by whether the ending sounds true instead of whether it actually follows from the premises. Seventy-one percent of participants judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid, which shows how easily good reasoning and truth get confused.

This is an example of a valid syllogism with a false conclusion, which shows that validity is not the same as truth. It has the same form as the birds, animals, eat food example, so it is valid. The conclusion that all birds have four legs is false only because the second premise, that all animals have four legs, is false.

No, this is not valid, even though every statement sounds reasonable. The problem is the word some. Saying some tired people are irritable leaves open which tired people they are, so all the students being tired does not place any of them among the irritable ones. The conclusion sounds believable, which is exactly why belief bias makes this easy to get wrong.

According to Johnson-Laird (1999), a mental model is a specific situation represented in a person's mind that can be used to help determine the validity of syllogisms in deductive reasoning. You build a picture of what the premises describe and reason from that picture. A model is one concrete way the premises could be true.

There are four steps. First, you create a model of the situation the premises describe. Second, you generate tentative conclusions about the model, meaning conclusions that might hold. Third, you look for exceptions that would falsify the model, searching for a case where the premises are true but the conclusion is not. Fourth, you determine the validity of the syllogism based on whether an exception turned up.

A conclusion is valid only if it cannot be refuted by any model of the premises. To refute it means showing it can be false. So if you can find even one model that fits the premises but not the conclusion, the conclusion does not follow and the syllogism is not valid. If none of the ways the premises could be true refutes it, then it is valid.

It helps because it shows how people reason by imagining a situation. In the pool table problem, you picture the black ball above the cue ball, the green ball to the right, and the red ball between them, and from that picture you work out that the cue ball is to the left of the line of sight. Most people solve it by imagining the arrangement, and that is the basis of the mental model proposal.

Modus ponens is the conditional syllogism that goes from p to q. If I study, I'll get a good grade, I studied, therefore I'll get a good grade. Since the condition is met, what follows from it has to follow too. It is valid, and 97 percent of participants judged it correctly. It moves forward, in the same direction as the rule, which is why it is the easiest of the four.

Modus tollens goes from not q to not p. If I study, I'll get a good grade, I didn't get a good grade, therefore I didn't study. It is valid, because if studying always leads to a good grade, a missing grade means the studying did not happen. It is harder because it runs backward, against the direction of the rule, and only 60 percent judged it correctly.

Because it runs from the result back to the condition, and the first premise never says that p is the only way to get q. If I live in Tucson, then I live in Arizona, and I live in Arizona, but that does not mean I live in Tucson. Someone can live in Arizona without living in Tucson, so the conclusion does not follow. Only 40 percent judged it correctly.

Because if p then q tells you what happens when p is true, but it says nothing about what happens when p is false. If I study, I'll get a good grade, and I didn't study, but I could still get a good grade some other way. So denying p settles nothing about q. This is the same kind of error as the previous one, from the other side, and again only 40 percent got it right.

The two valid ones are modus ponens and modus tollens. Modus ponens goes from p to q, and modus tollens goes from not q to not p. The two invalid ones go from q to p, and from not p to not q. The valid types confirm p or deny q, while the invalid types confirm q or deny p. People judged both valid ones correctly more often than both invalid ones, at 97 and 60 percent versus 40 percent each.

answers.topic: The Wason four-card problem and permission schemas
answers: You should turn over E and 7. To test the rule that a vowel on one side means an even number on the other, you look for cards that could break it. The E might hide an odd number, and the 7 might hide a vowel, and either would break the rule. The K is not a vowel, and the 4 can only fit the rule, so turning those two tests nothing.

The falsification principle says that to test a rule, you must look for situations that falsify the rule, which means situations that would prove it false. Most people do not do this. Instead of looking for what could break the rule, they go for cards that seem to fit it, which is why in the abstract problem 46 percent chose the 4 and only 7 percent chose the correct 7.

The rule was that if someone is drinking beer, then they must be 21 years old, and the cards read beer, soda, 16 years old and 21 years old. When the problem was put in concrete everyday terms, correct responses greatly increased, and 73 percent answered correctly. The right cards are beer and 16 years old, because someone drinking beer while under 21 is the only case that breaks the rule.

A permission schema is the idea that if A is satisfied, B can be carried out. It is a familiar pattern of knowledge about rules that grant permission once a condition is met. In the beer rule, being 21 is the condition and drinking beer is what can then be carried out. It tells people exactly what to check: the age of the beer drinker, and the drink of the sixteen-year-old.

The two versions have the same if-then form, but the abstract one is about letters and numbers and the concrete one is about familiar things. In the abstract version only 7 percent chose the correct 7 and 46 percent chose the 4. In the concrete version, 73 percent were correct. The concrete rule calls up a permission schema, and context matters, though familiarity alone does not explain the improvement.

The material says the student syllogism fails because of the word 'some'; the answer follows that wording.
